doc.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The flugelhorn: Miles's fat girl and rebuilding it for Selmer
summary: Miles, Berry and Rogers used flugelhorns with trumpet mouthpieces; Terry and Keith Eckert rebuilt one, the same horn Sykes Smith delivered.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns

blocks.x: We’ve talked a bit about the flugelhorn, but I want – now I want to concentrate some questions on that. Did you ever have an occasion to borrow a flugelhorn from Miles Davis or was that . . .

Yeah. Miles. As a matter of fact, Miles had his flugelhorn. He used to call it his fat girl. He’d say, “Hey, man, you ought to take my fat girl home with you. Try it, man. It’s mean.” Miles, Emmett Berry, and Shorty Rogers were three of the cats who had come upon flugelhorns. They were using trumpet mouthpieces in them, because you could play high with them. They’re larger tubing, “brrr.” They were screaming away on them. But

they didn’t really use them for the thing which they were built for, for a more mellifluous approach to playing. They didn’t use them for that. After I finally got Keith Eckert involved in trying to reconstruct one, when he was with Selmer – he was the technical adviser for brass at the Selmer Instrument Company. We finally put one together and hooked it up. I decided I was going to really try to do it like the old Lunceford band used to do. That’s where I first heard them. All three of them: Steve [Tommy Stevenson] and Sy Oliver and whatever the other trumpet player. They all used them. They used them for balance and nice little [Terry sings] tempo things like that. It was beautiful. This is what I had in mind when I was trying to – always trying to capture that sound. I would put a felt hat over the bell of my trumpet and try to grasp that flugelhorn sound, until finally Keith Eckert said, “Let’s try to put it back together.” So we tried some different tubings and so forth. Finally, we put the first one back together on the line for Selmer.
How does this relate to 1957 and the Duke Ellington experience of bringing . . .
This is just prior to that. We finally put that horn, that very horn together. Keith sent it back to Paris, and they did the final . . .
So that was the horn that was sent to your friend in Chicago.
So this is how the story gets connected.
Yeah. That’s the horn that you opened out of the case just now. That’s that horn, because I kept it and lent it – I lent it to the Ellington exhibit for the Smithsonian.
The “Beyond Category” exhibit the Smithsonian’s doing.
Yeah, and then I lent it to the Kansas City thing. They’re just sending it back. They made it look so pretty again, I want to start playing it again. It’s an old, old horn.
Would you then – it’s a fair statement that you were instrumental in the revitalization of the flugelhorn and its coming back on line to be manufactured. It was a dormant instrument, basically.

I don’t know. I don’t like to make statements like that. I don’t know. I just like the sound, and I want very much to get involved in it on – for my own. Of course other cats were getting involved for a different purpose. I wanted to get into that
mellifluousness of it. I don’t know whether you could say I was instrumental in it or not, but . . .
